title: Who Got Dee Pregnant?

jokes.text: Planning to use chalk and erasers to create a dust cloud so they can see the laser beam alarms in the museum — treating a Night at the Museum fantasy like a heist movie
jokes.setup: The gang is apparently planning to spend the night in a museum, ostensibly for a fun adventure
jokes.punchline: Frank's contribution is a tactically specific plan involving chalk dust to reveal laser beam security alarms, treating a childish fantasy with heist-level seriousness
jokes.explanation: The joke works because Frank treats the museum sleepover with the tactical seriousness of a professional thief. His total commitment to the bit (specific tools: chalk AND erasers) elevates it above a simple absurdist non-sequitur.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I think we should get some chalk and some erasers, because that dust cloud, you know, really shows the laser beam alarms.

jokes.text: Dennis's sincere speech about 'opening themselves up to the possibility of an amazing adventure' and 'ancient spirits' — delivered completely earnestly by a man who is clearly too old and self-important for this
jokes.setup: The gang is planning to break into a museum overnight like children excited about a movie premise
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a grandiose, sincere monologue about 'opening ourselves up to the possibility of an amazing adventure' as if he's a profound philosopher, not a grown man sneaking into a museum to avoid his pregnant sister
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis self-aggrandizement — he elevates a childish plan into something noble. The character integration is strong because only Dennis would deliver this with such unearned gravitas.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We got to spend a lot of time in the Civil War section.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: No, we're not doing the Civil War section, Frank.

jokes.text: 'It's fatness, Frank, plain and simple. It's a person becoming fat before your eyes.'
jokes.setup: Frank comments that Dee has been 'stuffing her face for days'
jokes.punchline: Dennis delivers a mock-clinical diagnosis — 'It's fatness, Frank, plain and simple' — as if he's a doctor explaining a rare condition, when he's just being cruel to his sister
jokes.explanation: The clinical framing ('plain and simple,' 'before your eyes') is what makes this land. Dennis isn't just insulting Dee — he's narrating her fatness like a nature documentary. High economy, strong character voice. Quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: I don't even know how to make the bird jokes anymore, like they don't apply.

jokes.text: 'I don't even really know how to make the bird jokes anymore. Like, they don't apply.'
jokes.setup: The gang is used to mocking Dee by calling her a bird; now she's visibly pregnant
jokes.punchline: Mac is genuinely distressed that pregnancy has disrupted his bird-joke routine — his concern is for his own joke material, not for Dee
jokes.explanation: This is a brilliant piece of character work. Mac's selfishness is so complete that pregnancy — a major life event — registers only as an inconvenience to his insult repertoire. The phrasing 'they don't apply' treats cruelty as craft. Strong character integration, great economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I'm not fat. I'm pregnant.

jokes.text: 'I'm not fat. I'm pregnant.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Dennis have been mocking Dee for being fat for the entire opening scene
jokes.punchline: Dee drops the revelation that she's pregnant, recontextualizing all the fat jokes that just preceded
jokes.explanation: Perfect economy — four words that reframe everything. The timing is good and the structure works as a classic reversal. The rewatch bonus is high because on rewatch the bird jokes in this scene take on a different texture. Not wildly original but structurally efficient.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I feel like you say that all the time now.

jokes.text: 'You better do yourself a favor and flush it out.'
jokes.setup: Dee announces she is pregnant
jokes.punchline: Frank's immediate, matter-of-fact response is to suggest abortion with zero emotional sensitivity — 'flush it out' as if discussing a clogged drain
jokes.explanation: The humor is in the total absence of human warmth. 'Flush it out' is perfect Frank — plumbing metaphor, no euphemism, no hesitation. High economy and character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: You better do yourself a favor and flush it out.

jokes.text: 'Dee, we don't care about you or your body or your baby or that baby bird that you're probably carrying inside of you.'
jokes.setup: The gang has been dismissive of Dee; Dennis summarizes their collective position
jokes.punchline: Dennis's list of things they don't care about keeps escalating until it arrives at 'that baby bird that you're probably carrying inside of you' — the bird insult applied to a fetus
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the list ('you, your body, your baby') and then the pivot to 'baby bird' is well-structured. It's also absurd — extrapolating the bird insult to prenatal level shows how committed the gang is to the bit over basic human decency.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Dee, we don't care about you or your body, or your baby, or that baby bird you're probably carrying inside of you.

jokes.text: Dee drops the bombshell that one of them is the father, then calmly says 'Hey, have a great time, guys' and waves them off to the museum
jokes.setup: The gang dismisses Dee's pregnancy; she reveals one of them is the father — which should be a huge dramatic moment
jokes.punchline: Dee immediately deflates the tension by cheerfully sending them off to the museum as if she said nothing — the juxtaposition of the bombshell and the breezy send-off
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural beat. The escalation to 'one of you is the father' followed by the immediate, cheerful 'Hey, have a great time, guys' is a masterclass in comedic deflation. The cut to [01:37] 'Oh, shit' makes this even better.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Well you should give a shit, 'cause one of you is the father.

jokes.text: Beat of silence followed by a single 'Oh, shit.' — the gang's collective reaction to Dee's paternity reveal
jokes.setup: Dee has just casually revealed one of the gang is the father of her baby and left
jokes.punchline: A long beat of silence, then one deflated 'Oh, shit.' — the understatement of the year
jokes.explanation: The beat works because of its restraint. After Dee's bomb, the entire gang's existential panic is summed up in two words. Great economy — the gap between the [01:20] and [02:13] scenes implies the stunned silence.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: What?

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: W-What the hell you talking about?

jokes.text: 'I browned out that evening.' / 'Browned out? What's browned out?' / 'Oh, it's when you drink so much that everything goes brown. It's not as severe as a blackout.'
jokes.setup: The gang is trying to reconstruct the Halloween party; Mac says he doesn't remember because he 'browned out'
jokes.punchline: Mac has coined a new term — 'browning out' — a lesser version of a blackout where 'everything goes brown,' delivered with total confidence as if it's a recognized medical phenomenon
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's standout jokes. 'Browning out' is a brilliantly original term — the logical extension of blackout into a lesser, browner state of inebriation. Mac's confidence in defining it, Frank's earnest clarification question, and the gang's subsequent embrace of the term make this a multi-beat gem. Highly quotable and spawns a running gag.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I-I browned out that evening.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Browned out? What's browned out?

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Oh, it's when you drink so much that everything goes brown. It's not as severe as a blackout, 'cause I remember bits and pieces. I like to call it browning out.

jokes.text: Dennis's meta-commentary: 'There's a good reason for that, Frank — because I think Mac just made it up on the spot.' / Mac: 'I did.' / 'You did. That's a great term.'
jokes.setup: Frank questions whether 'browning out' is a real term
jokes.punchline: Dennis correctly identifies that Mac invented the term on the spot; Mac admits it without shame; Dennis then endorses it anyway
jokes.explanation: The self-aware acknowledgment that Mac invented the term — followed by immediate collective adoption — is a lovely meta-beat. The gang knows it's absurd and doesn't care. Character-specific: only this gang would do this.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: There's a good reason for that, Frank. Because I think Mac just made it up on the spot.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I did.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You did?

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: That's a great term... browning out.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You like it?

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: I love it!

jokes.text: Charlie's escalating 'brown' compound: 'put our browns together, mash them together' — immediately followed by Dennis warning not to overuse it
jokes.setup: The gang has just adopted 'browning out' as official terminology
jokes.punchline: Charlie immediately overextends the metaphor ('put our browns together, mash them together'), Dennis checks him — 'let's not overuse the brown thing right in the beginning' — breaking the fourth wall of their own bit
jokes.explanation: The joke is in Dennis managing the bit in real time — he's the writers' room inside the show, warning against joke fatigue. Then Mac immediately announces he'll 'probably use it a lot right now.' Perfect escalation of the meta-commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Once you throw a term like that out and everybody likes it, it's pretty much fair game.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: We can use it whenever...

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: It's public domain at that point.

jokes.text: Mac and Dennis's argument over breaking their 'funny over sexy' costume pact — 'Without my Mario, what am I? I'm just some weird Italian plumber. I look like an asshole.'
jokes.setup: Mac reveals he held up his end of a Mario/Luigi costume agreement; Dennis arrived in a different 'sexy' costume
jokes.punchline: 'Without my Mario, what am I? I'm just some weird Italian plumber. I look like an asshole.' — Mac's Mario costume is only intelligible with a Luigi present; alone he's just a man dressed as a plumber
jokes.explanation: Genuinely funny observation about couples costumes — the Mario without Luigi problem is real and relatable. Mac's existential crisis ('what am I?') about his costume identity is perfectly in character. 'I look like an asshole' is a great button. High quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I'm that character from Lord of the Rings, Viggio Morgenstein.

jokes.text: 'I'm that character from Lord of the Rings, Viggio Morgenstein.'
jokes.setup: Dennis shows up in a different costume; Mac asks what it even is
jokes.punchline: Dennis confidently names his costume as 'Viggio Morgenstein' — conflating the actor Viggo Mortensen with his character Aragorn, getting both completely wrong
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Dennis's confident, specific wrongness — 'Viggio Morgenstein' — is perfect. He collapses actor and character into one mangled name. The specificity of the error (not just 'some guy from Lord of the Rings' but a specific wrong name) makes it exceptional. It immediately becomes a callback throughout the episode. This is Dennis's particular brand of confident stupidity. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Okay, that is not the character's name, that's the actor's name, and you're not even getting that right.

jokes.text: 'Okay, that is not the character's name. That's the actor's name. And you're not even getting that right.'
jokes.setup: Dennis announces his costume is 'Viggio Morgenstein' from Lord of the Rings
jokes.punchline: Mac's correction is two-layered: (1) that's the actor, not the character, and (2) you're mispronouncing the actor's name anyway
jokes.explanation: The double correction — wrong name category AND wrong pronunciation — lands perfectly. The structure is clean: setup error, two-beat correction. Mac's deadpan delivery of 'and you're not even getting that right' is the button.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Fizz! Fizz! I vant to suck your blood! It's Tvilight time! Time for blood sucking.

jokes.text: Charlie arrives at the Halloween party dressed as the Phantom of the Opera and announces 'I want to suck your blood! It's Twilight time! Time for blood sucking.'
jokes.setup: Charlie is trying to appeal to girls who like vampires due to Twilight; he chose the Phantom of the Opera as his vampire costume
jokes.punchline: Charlie enters doing a vampire shtick in a Phantom of the Opera costume, calling it 'Twilight time' — completely unaware he's not a vampire
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie — his logic is internally consistent (vampires are popular, I want a sexy vampire costume, the Phantom is kind of dark and mysterious) but completely wrong. His enthusiasm in declaring 'It's Twilight time!' while dressed as a theater-haunting composer is quintessential Charlie Day energy.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You are dressed like the Phantom of the Opera. He's not a vampire. He eats theater people.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, he doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I think he might.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He does.

jokes.text: 'You are dressed like the Phantom of the Opera. He's not a vampire. He eats theater people.' / 'No, he doesn't.' / 'I think he might.' / 'He does.' / 'He might not.' / 'He doesn't.' / 'No, I don't. I don't.'
jokes.setup: Mac points out Charlie's Phantom of the Opera is not a vampire
jokes.punchline: The gang devolves into a ridiculous debate about whether the Phantom eats theater people, with nobody actually knowing and Charlie ultimately confirming he has no idea who the Phantom is
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best exchanges. The rapid-fire back-and-forth about whether the Phantom 'eats theater people,' ending with Charlie admitting he doesn't know who the Phantom is, is perfectly constructed. The escalation from wrong to more wrong to 'I don't. I don't.' is a classic Always Sunny rhythm. Dennis being surprised Charlie knows who the Phantom is, then immediately confirmed wrong, is a great extra beat.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: And I'm surprised you even know who the Phantom of the Opera is.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: He might not.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: He doesn't.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: No, I don't, I don't.

jokes.text: 'This party blows. There's no studs here. No beef in the freezer, if you know what I mean.'
jokes.setup: Dee arrives at the Halloween party in an angel costume
jokes.punchline: Dee's meat-market assessment of the party — 'no beef in the freezer' — is delivered with the worldliness of someone who has been to many disappointing parties, while wearing angel wings
jokes.explanation: Decent Dee line — the meat metaphor is a bit broad but the delivery context (angel wings) adds irony. Not one of the sharper jokes in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: There's no studs here. No beef in the freezer, if you know what I mean.

jokes.text: 'Dee, why in God's name would you wear a costume with giant wings?' — followed by the gang refusing to acknowledge she's a sexy angel, insisting she looks like a bird
jokes.setup: Dee arrives in a 'sexy angel' costume with large wings
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately frames her as a bird — their default mode — ignoring the 'sexy' part entirely and focusing on the bird silhouette
jokes.explanation: Good running gag payoff — the bird jokes applied to her Halloween costume is a natural extension. Structurally serves the episode's later twist (her switching costumes with the peacock girl).

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Are we supposed to pretend like you're not dressed like a giant bird? I mean, if you're gonna be sexy, don't dress like a bird, Dee.

jokes.text: The gang spots the peacock girl: 'Did you guys see that cooze over there dressing like a peacock? Big, giant bird. Green bird.' — immediately followed by all three men ogling her
jokes.setup: Dee is upset that the gang is calling her a bird because of her angel wings
jokes.punchline: Dee herself spots a 'cooze' in a peacock costume, calls it a 'big giant green bird' — then the men immediately switch from mocking Dee's birdness to lusting after the peacock girl for the exact same quality
jokes.explanation: Smart structural joke — the same bird-ness that makes Dee a mockery makes the peacock girl desirable. The hypocrisy is the punchline. 'She wears it well / She wears it very well' as the men immediately reverse their position is nicely constructed.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: She wears it well. Woof, woof. She wears it very well.

jokes.text: 'She wears it so well, in fact, that I have now pinpointed her as my prey for the evening.'
jokes.setup: Dennis is attracted to the peacock costume girl
jokes.punchline: 'Pinpointed her as my prey' — Dennis's predatory self-description, delivered with complete earnestness, as if hunting women is a normal and dignified thing to announce
jokes.explanation: Classic Dennis — the serial-killer undertone played completely straight. 'Pinpointed as my prey' is a phrase no normal human would use about romantic interest, but Dennis says it like it's the most natural thing in the world. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: despite looking like a cartoon bricklayer I was started to get pretty close to sealing the deal with the peacock lady.

jokes.text: Mac shoves Dee aside saying 'Out of my way, bird.' while charging toward the peacock girl
jokes.setup: Mac is eager to pursue the peacock girl
jokes.punchline: He literally shoves Dee out of his path with 'Out of my way, bird' — both using the bird insult dismissively and treating her like an obstacle
jokes.explanation: Quick, functional gag. 'Out of my way, bird' is economical cruelty. The physical dismissal reinforces the gang's treatment of Dee as an obstacle rather than a person.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: She's like... 'Oh, my God, you look so sexy. I'm gonna sex you all up.' 'Oh, my goodness... Get your sex off me!'

jokes.text: Mac describes himself in the Mario costume as 'looking like a cartoon bricklayer' while trying to seduce a woman
jokes.setup: Mac in a Mario costume is trying to seduce the peacock girl
jokes.punchline: Mac acknowledges he looks like 'a cartoon bricklayer' — the most unflattering accurate description of Mario — while still being confident he's about to 'seal the deal'
jokes.explanation: 'Cartoon bricklayer' is an inspired way to describe Mario — technically accurate, maximally unflattering. The gap between Mac's self-awareness about the costume and his confidence about sealing the deal is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: You have any idea what it's like to be this sexy?

jokes.text: Charlie's version: the peacock girl is forcibly attracted to him — 'She's like, oh my God, you look so sexy! I'm gonna sex you all up! I'm like, you're just my friend! Get your sex off me!'
jokes.setup: Charlie (in the Phantom costume) claims a woman was taking sexual advantage of him
jokes.punchline: Charlie's retelling positions him as an unwilling victim of female desire — 'Get your sex off me!' — the inverse of how these situations actually happen, delivered with genuine distress
jokes.explanation: Brilliantly Charlie. His fantasy is not that he's a romantic hero but that he's a reluctant sex object being pursued against his will. 'Get your sex off me!' is a perfect, original line — the indignation, the phrasing, the complete inversion of expectation. This is high-quality character comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Waitress
dialogue.line: Yeah, Charlie, I received all 100 of them.

jokes.text: 'You have any idea what it's like to be this sexy?'
jokes.setup: Charlie is lamenting being taken advantage of in his Phantom of the Opera costume
jokes.punchline: Charlie asks if anyone understands the burden of being 'this sexy' — Charlie Kelly, in a Phantom of the Opera costume, sincerely believing he is overwhelmingly attractive
jokes.explanation: Charlie's sincere delivery of this complaint is the joke. The gap between Charlie's self-image and reality is a classic Always Sunny engine. Good economy.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: I made out with the waitress! That's amazing!

jokes.text: Mac happily accepts the Phantom costume and claims it was his plan all along — 'Yes, dude! It's all coming back to me now. You came over to me. We agreed to switch costumes.'
jokes.setup: Mac in the Mario costume has been struggling; Charlie offers to switch with his Phantom costume
jokes.punchline: Mac immediately reframes the situation as a victory for himself — 'I was able to fell the seductive temptress finally' — his ego requiring that every outcome be his triumph
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — 'fell the seductive temptress' is a Mac-ism. The costume switch is the key plot mechanic, so this serves both comedy and story well.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: First of all, don't say I went as Spider-Man. I didn't go as Spider-Man. I was Man-Spider. Totally different.

jokes.text: 'Well, mystery solved. I mean — Awesome!' — Dennis declaring victory after learning Mac had sex with the peacock girl, completely missing that this doesn't answer the paternity question
jokes.setup: Mac reveals he had sex with the peacock girl after the costume switch
jokes.punchline: Dennis enthusiastically declares 'Mystery solved!' — genuinely forgetting the actual mystery is who impregnated Dee
jokes.explanation: Classic Always Sunny — the gang getting distracted by irrelevant details. Dennis genuinely solving the wrong mystery with 'Mystery solved!' captures their collective self-absorption perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: She incorporated a bun in the lovemaking. She took the-the... the dough and rolled it up into a ball, and then she... And we were going berserk.

jokes.text: 'Who wouldn't feel that way after banging — Ah, shit, dude. Oh, shit.' — Dennis nearly says something horrible about Dee before catching himself, then realizing the implication
jokes.setup: Mac suggests Charlie must be the father because of his emotional reaction (tears)
jokes.punchline: Dennis begins a Dee-disparagement mid-sentence, stops himself, then realizes what it implies about who actually did it
jokes.explanation: The broken sentence is key — Dennis can't even complete an insult about Dee without the horror of its implication dawning on him. Good structural use of the incomplete sentence as a comedic device.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Frank, Frank, we don't need to hear this part of the story. Okay? Can you just tell us about Halloween? Stick to Halloween night.

jokes.text: Charlie insisting 'No. Those were tears of joy.' about the tears he was shedding after (allegedly) sleeping with Dee
jokes.setup: Mac interprets Charlie's remembered tears as remorse/regret over sleeping with Dee
jokes.punchline: Charlie insists they were 'tears of joy' — a correction that actually makes the situation worse and more absurd
jokes.explanation: The 'tears of joy' correction is a great escalation — it doesn't exonerate Charlie, it just changes the valence of his alleged crime to something even weirder. The delivery is key.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Not from you! It's the stupid sexy costume.

jokes.text: The waitress arrives: 'Yeah, Charlie, I received all 100 of them.' — responding to Charlie's claim he 'invited' her
jokes.setup: Charlie announces 'Hey, I see you received my invitation' as the waitress walks in
jokes.punchline: She clarifies she received all 100 of his invitations — Charlie sent 100 identical invitations to one person, which is stalker behavior presented as normal
jokes.explanation: Perfect Charlie/Waitress dynamic — Charlie's pathological persistence expressed through the mundane act of sending 100 party invitations. The Waitress saying it so flatly is great. Strong character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: I don't remember most evenings.

jokes.text: Mac gets a gallon of milk spilled on him during the bar fight — 'Oh, goddamn it! I got milk all over me!'
jokes.setup: A bar fight breaks out when Mac tries to defend Charlie's honor against the Waitress's boyfriend
jokes.punchline: Mac's tough-guy fight ends not with a knockout but with him being drenched in the McPoyles' milk — a signature absurd detail from Always Sunny lore
jokes.explanation: The milk is perfect Always Sunny — the McPoyles' grotesque milk-drinking habit weaponized as comedy. The fight ending in dairy humiliation rather than glory is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: Because it's really interesting and innovative, and I thought maybe you'd want some lessons.

jokes.text: Charlie observes the milk-drenched Mac: 'That... was insanely masculine.'
jokes.setup: Mac has just been showered in McPoyle milk during a failed bar fight
jokes.punchline: 'That... was insanely masculine' — delivered with complete earnestness, the gap between Mac being covered in milk and 'insanely masculine' being the entire joke
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's most quotable lines. The pause before 'was' and the deadpan delivery make this land. 'Insanely masculine' as a descriptor for being covered in milk is a perfect ironic understatement. The line is later echoed (callback), which shows its structural importance.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: I'm talking about the sounds of hot, passionate lovemaking that was coming from the bathroom that I had heard with my own two ear balls.

jokes.text: Frank corrects the record: 'First of all, don't say I went as Spider-Man. I didn't go as Spider-Man. I was Man-Spider. Totally different!'
jokes.setup: Frank begins to correct Charlie's version of Halloween events
jokes.punchline: 'I was Man-Spider' — Frank's costume distinction is the inversion of Spider-Man (a man who is a spider vs. a spider that is a man), which Frank treats as a profound difference
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes and a true Always Sunny classic. 'Man-Spider. Totally different!' is brilliantly original — the word-reversal of Spider-Man into Man-Spider, Frank's absolute conviction that this distinction matters, and the economical delivery make this exceptional. Comparable in quality to the 8.0 anchor and arguably better in terms of quotability and originality. This line transcends the episode.

dialogue.speaker: Artemis
dialogue.line: where we gave each other handjobs.

jokes.text: Frank's Wendy's Dumpster sex story: 'we had some makeup sex in a Dumpster out in the back of Wendy's. She incorporated a bun in the lovemaking.'
jokes.setup: Frank begins explaining why he and Artemis were arguing at the Halloween party
jokes.punchline: Frank casually reveals he had sex in a Dumpster behind Wendy's and Artemis incorporated a hamburger bun into the act — delivered with the nostalgic warmth of a fond memory
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in character for Frank and Artemis — two of the show's grossest characters engaged in Dumpster sex with fast-food bread products. The specificity of 'behind Wendy's' and 'a hamburger bun' makes this exceptional. Frank's warm delivery of this horror is key. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Mac's the dad! Do it with me. Mac's the dad!

jokes.text: Frank's graphic elaboration: 'She took the dough and rolled it up into a ball, and then she — We were going berserk. She loves that kind of stuff.'
jokes.setup: Frank has already described Dumpster sex with a hamburger bun
jokes.punchline: Frank begins to graphically describe what Artemis did with the bun, escalating until Dennis has to stop him
jokes.explanation: The escalation of the bun description — cut off before the reveal — is a great use of the incomplete sentence. The audience's imagination does the work. 'We were going berserk' as a summary is perfect Frank understatement.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: There was no time for an ocular pat-down.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Frank, we don't need to hear this part of the story, okay? Can you just tell us about Halloween? Stick to Halloween night.'
jokes.setup: Frank is enthusiastically elaborating on the Dumpster sex
jokes.punchline: Dennis, usually the least squeamish of the gang, is visibly desperate to end this story — his discomfort is the joke
jokes.explanation: Functional straight-man beat — Dennis pumping the brakes on Frank's oversharing. Works mainly as a setup for Frank continuing anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: I had a tremendous amount of douche bag blood all over my knuckles

jokes.text: Mac's unreliable memory version: he punches the boyfriend, gets milk on him, and Charlie says 'Insanely masculine' — a beat-for-beat replay of the earlier scene with Mac as the heroic version of himself
jokes.setup: Mac is now giving his version of the Halloween fight
jokes.punchline: Mac's version of events is essentially identical to Charlie's except Mac is the hero — the milk scene replays but now Mac is 'insanely masculine' as the instigator
jokes.explanation: The repeated beat works as a Rashomon joke — same events, different hero. Mac's self-aggrandizing retelling is in character. The 'insanely masculine' callback lands well because it now confirms Charlie was complimenting Mac's violence, not the milk situation.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Shoo. Shoo! Get out of here. Shoo. Shoo. Shoo. Come on. Get out. Get out.

jokes.text: Mac's dramatic monologue: 'There was no time for an ocular pat-down.'
jokes.setup: Mac is explaining why he immediately jumped into the bar fight to defend Charlie
jokes.punchline: 'There was no time for an ocular pat-down' — Mac uses his invented tactical terminology for visually assessing a threat, treating a bar fight as a military operation
jokes.explanation: One of Mac's best lines. 'Ocular pat-down' is a perfect Mac-ism — he's invented tactical terminology that sounds vaguely plausible but is entirely his own. The gravity with which he announces there was 'no time' for it is perfect character comedy. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: Margaret, what are you doing here? God, that is so gross. You're always doing that. Are you trying to tell me something? Ugh. Is that, like, a sexual thing? All right, let's do this.

jokes.text: 'I don't remember that night.' / 'I didn't tell you which night yet.' / 'I don't remember most evenings.'
jokes.setup: The gang asks Artemis if she remembers a specific night
jokes.punchline: Before they name the night, Artemis preemptively claims not to remember it — then clarifies she doesn't remember 'most evenings,' revealing the scope of her amnesia
jokes.explanation: Structurally very clean. The setup-punchline-escalation is perfectly compressed: (1) I don't remember, (2) I haven't told you which night, (3) I don't remember most evenings. The escalation reveals a character detail (Artemis's blackout lifestyle) with beautiful economy. One of the best-structured exchanges in the episode.

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: Your breath is awful.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: Artemis explains why her Wendy's Dumpster sex is 'interesting and innovative' and offers to give the gang 'lessons'
jokes.setup: The gang tries to redirect Artemis away from the Dumpster sex story
jokes.punchline: Artemis genuinely believes her Dumpster/hamburger-bun technique is 'interesting and innovative' and offers lessons — she considers herself a sexual innovator
jokes.explanation: Artemis's total lack of shame is her defining trait. Offering lessons in Dumpster sex technique is in perfect character. The callback to the bun story compounds the cringe.

dialogue.speaker: Liam McPoyle
dialogue.line: Your breath is awful.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Really?

dialogue.speaker: Liam McPoyle
dialogue.line: Yeah.

jokes.text: 'Oh, well, that makes sense. Mac slept with her at the party.' — Artemis casually dropping the paternity accusation
jokes.setup: The gang asks if Artemis remembers anything about Dee getting pregnant
jokes.punchline: Artemis drops the name 'Mac' with complete casualness — 'that makes sense' — as if it's the most natural conclusion in the world
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the casual delivery of a bombshell accusation. 'That makes sense' as if it's completely obvious is a good Artemis moment.

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: Viggio Morgenstein! Hey. I'm insanely high on mescaline.

jokes.text: Artemis explains what she 'heard' from outside the bathroom: 'the passionate, unmistakable sounds of lovemaking coming from inside'
jokes.setup: Artemis overheard noises from the locked bathroom and concluded Mac and Dee were having sex
jokes.punchline: Artemis describing bathroom noises as 'passionate, unmistakable sounds of lovemaking' — her romantic framing of what were probably just gross bathroom sounds
jokes.explanation: Functional plot beat. The humor is in Artemis's confidence about what she heard and her romantic language for it. Moderate.

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: I heard you gave quite a performance, Macwell.

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: Mm... Mm... mmm...

jokes.text: Artemis reveals she and Frank 'had to sneak outside to my station wagon where we gave each other hand jobs.'
jokes.setup: Frank and Artemis couldn't use the men's room for their makeup sex because the door was locked
jokes.punchline: Their romantic alternative was mutual hand jobs in Artemis's station wagon — delivered as if this is a reasonable and dignified fallback plan
jokes.explanation: Perfect Always Sunny Frank/Artemis beat. The specificity ('station wagon') and the matter-of-factness of 'gave each other hand jobs' as a Plan B make this land hard. The audience is both grossed out and laughing — classic cringe comedy done well.

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: She's still expecting a call.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: That's not going to happen.

dialogue.speaker: McPoyle
dialogue.line: You will call her!

jokes.text: Charlie enthusiastically declares 'Mac's the dad! Chant with me. Mac's the dad!' and tries to get the group to chant
jokes.setup: Artemis's testimony appears to implicate Mac as Dee's baby's father
jokes.punchline: Charlie's response to this serious paternity revelation is to try to start a chant — 'Chant with me' — treating a family crisis like a sporting event
jokes.explanation: Perfectly Charlie — his response to any dramatic revelation is enthusiasm and crowd participation. 'Chant with me' in this context is absurdly inappropriate and therefore hilarious. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Listen, all right, number one, it's a win-win for both of us. That weird plumber... he's going to leave you alone for the rest of the night. That's good, right? And then the second great thing for you is I'm not going to beat the shit out of you, so let's go.

jokes.text: Mac to Dee in the bathroom: 'I don't give a shit about your problems, Dee. I'm still pumped up from that ass-whooping I just handed out. Did you see that?'
jokes.setup: Dee enters the men's bathroom upset that she's covered in milk
jokes.punchline: Mac is so intoxicated by his own violence that he literally cannot process Dee's presence — he immediately pivots to 'Did you see that?' seeking validation
jokes.explanation: Good Mac moment — his narcissism expressed through post-fight validation-seeking. 'Did you see that?' when Dee is literally standing there covered in milk is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: Call me a bird all night. Making fun, saying names. Well, let's see who's sexy now, dickwads. 'Cause I look good.

jokes.text: Mac shoos Dee out of the bathroom: 'Shoo. Shoo. Get out of here. Shoo. Shoo! Get out! Get out! So annoying.'
jokes.setup: Mac wants Dee out of the bathroom
jokes.punchline: Mac shoos Dee like a stray animal — 'Shoo. Shoo.' — the repetition of 'shoo' escalating as if she's a pigeon he's trying to get off a bench
jokes.explanation: The 'shoo' repetition escalating is physically funny — Mac treating Dee as vermin. Works especially well because it rhymes with the bird-running gag (shooing a 'bird').

dialogue.speaker: Charlie
dialogue.line: So Dee thinks that I'm the dad, but, Dennis, you're the dad.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Delightful.

jokes.text: Mac shoos Dee out of the bathroom like a stray animal: 'Shoo. Shoo. Get out of here. Shoo! Shoo! Shoo! Come on! Get out! Get out! So annoying.'
jokes.setup: Mac is trying to get Dee out of the men's bathroom
jokes.punchline: Mac literally shoos Dee as if she's a pigeon or a dog — the dehumanizing act delivered with the casual irritation of someone dealing with a minor pest
jokes.explanation: The 'shoo' escalation — from one 'shoo' to a rapid-fire series of them — is well-executed. The dehumanizing animal-shooing applied to Dee connects to the bird running gag without being an explicit bird joke. 'So annoying' as a button is good. Mac's cruelty as casual habit.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Don't flush.

jokes.text: Knock, knock: Artemis enters saying 'Knock, knock, dick-faces.'
jokes.setup: The gang is meeting to piece together Halloween night
jokes.punchline: Artemis announces her arrival with 'Knock, knock, dick-faces' — treating a standard greeting as an opportunity for aggression
jokes.explanation: Perfect Artemis entrance. 'Knock, knock, dick-faces' is three words that do a lot of work — the parody of the greeting formula, the casual insult. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: We got to get you and that monster that's in your gut down to Mexico ASAP.

jokes.text: Mac turns around and Margaret McPoyle is in the bathroom, and he treats her sudden appearance as a possible 'sexual thing'
jokes.setup: Mac has just successfully expelled Dee from the bathroom
jokes.punchline: 'Whoa! Margaret, what are you doing here? God, that is so gross. You're always doing that. Are you trying to tell me something? Is that, like, a sexual thing?'
jokes.explanation: Mac's read of Margaret's gross behavior as potentially sexual — and his immediate pivot to 'All right. Let's do this' — is a good reveal of Mac's specific brand of delusional sexual confidence. The 'you're always doing that' implies a history with Margaret that makes it funnier.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: I just told you that because you were making fun of me for eating the sandwich, and I thought it would upset you and get you going and it did, it worked.

jokes.text: Mac: 'All right. Let's do this.' — deciding to sleep with Margaret McPoyle
jokes.setup: Mac has evaluated Margaret's gross bathroom appearance as a possible sexual overture
jokes.punchline: His immediate, businesslike 'All right. Let's do this.' — no further deliberation, no romance, just a tactical decision
jokes.explanation: Four words, maximum efficiency. Mac's 'let's do this' applied to sex with Margaret McPoyle sounds like he's about to bench-press. The absence of any deliberation, excitement, or disgust — just pure operational readiness — is very funny and very Mac. High economy.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Oh! Whew!

jokes.text: 'Viggio Morgenstein!' — called out during the Halloween fight flashback as a battle cry
jokes.setup: The Halloween fight is replaying in the McPoyle version
jokes.punchline: Charlie (in the Phantom/Man-Spider crossover of costumes) shouts 'Viggio Morgenstein!' as a war cry during the bar fight — using the wrong name as a battle shout
jokes.explanation: One of the best callbacks in the episode. The name 'Viggio Morgenstein' — already established as a ridiculous wrong name — deployed as a battle cry is inspired. It's the most Charlie possible use of a Lord of the Rings reference. Perfect economy (two words) and great structural payoff of the earlier costume joke.

dialogue.speaker: Dee
dialogue.line: but I'll tell you what, I'm not going to tell you who the father is.

jokes.text: McPoyle reveals: 'I'm insanely high on mescaline.'
jokes.setup: The McPoyle brothers are supposedly sober witnesses (they only drink milk), making them the most reliable narrators of the night
jokes.punchline: One McPoyle reveals he was 'insanely high on mescaline' that night — their sobriety was false all along, undermining their credibility as witnesses
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural payoff. The gang's entire theory rested on the McPoyles being 'stone-cold sober' (the milk = sobriety assumption). The reveal that one was on mescaline collapses this logic beautifully. Delivered with McPoyle's trademark deadpan. High economy — four words destroy the narrative foundation. One of the episode's best structural jokes.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: This close... ...man, I really dodged the bullet on that.

jokes.text: Mac's horror: 'Are you telling me that wasn't even the waitress?'
jokes.setup: The McPoyles reveal the woman who 'made out with Charlie' was not the waitress
jokes.punchline: Mac's first concern, upon learning the whole story is wrong, is whether Mac kissed the waitress — his reaction reveals the entire story was filtered through self-interest
jokes.explanation: Good character beat — Mac's immediate concern about the wrong detail reveals his self-centered perspective. Functional but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You look like a turkey.

dialogue.speaker: Dennis
dialogue.line: Yeah. Also I would say, I would say you look like an-an ostrich.

dialogue.speaker: Frank
dialogue.line: Yes!

dialogue.speaker: Mac
dialogue.line: You know, I was... I want to call her an emu, but I want to save it for, you know... You are big, fat, flightless bird.

jokes.text: Ryan McPoyle reveals: 'Are you telling me that wasn't even the waitress?' — having believed throughout the whole story that Charlie/Dennis was talking to the waitress
jokes.setup: In Charlie's version of events, he was interacting with the waitress at the party
jokes.punchline: The McPoyle reveals the woman wasn't the waitress at all — Charlie (or the person in the Charlie costume) was talking to a completely different woman this whole time, implying Charlie's 'made out with the waitress' was entirely fabricated
jokes.explanation: A good structural reveal that retroactively recontextualizes Charlie's narration. The confirmation that Charlie hallucinated/fabricated the waitress encounter is consistent with his unreliable narrator status and his obsession. Good plot-comedy integration.

jokes.text: McPoyle narration: 'Mac kicked her out of the bathroom so he could make sweet love to Margaret in private.' — pause — Mmm. Mmm! Mmm! Oh!
jokes.setup: The McPoyle brother is narrating what happened in the bathroom
jokes.punchline: After matter-of-factly announcing Mac made sweet love to Margaret, Margaret herself makes increasingly enthusiastic 'Mmm' sounds while presumably eating or remembering — a grotesque endorsement
jokes.explanation: Margaret McPoyle's wordless escalating 'Mmm! Mmm! Oh!' in response to the mention of her encounter with Mac is brilliantly uncomfortable. It's the most she's ever communicated. The gang's horrified reaction ('Okay, that's enough') and Dennis's 'God, that's your sister' adds a layer. The structure is excellent — the matter-of-fact narration punctuated by Margaret's visceral enthusiasm is a great comedic contrast.

jokes.text: McPoyle on Mac's bathroom performance: 'I heard you gave quite a performance, Macwell.'
jokes.setup: The McPoyle reveals Mac locked himself in the bathroom with Margaret McPoyle
jokes.punchline: 'I heard you gave quite a performance, Macwell' — the McPoyle's deadpan acknowledgment of his sister's sex life, delivered without apparent discomfort
jokes.explanation: The McPoyle's complete lack of normal reaction to his sister's sex life is characteristically creepy-funny. 'Quite a performance, Macwell' has a Victorian formality that makes it funnier.

jokes.text: Margaret McPoyle's orgasmic sounds — 'Mmm. Mmm! Mmm! Oh!' — in reaction to learning Mac had sex with her
jokes.setup: Mac is confirmed to have had sex with Margaret McPoyle in the Halloween bathroom
jokes.punchline: Margaret McPoyle (who is mute) responds to this revelation with escalating sexual noises — 'Mmm... Mmm! Oh!' — in front of the entire gang
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's great cringe beats. Margaret's mute sexual enthusiasm in front of her brother and the entire gang is perfectly executed horror-comedy. The escalation of 'Mmm' to 'Oh!' while everyone watches is exquisitely uncomfortable. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: Mac: 'Okay, that's enough, all right? God, that's your sister.' / McPoyle brother showing zero reaction
jokes.setup: Margaret is making escalating sexual sounds about Mac
jokes.punchline: Mac has to remind the McPoyle brother that 'that's your sister' — the McPoyle's total nonreaction to his sister's public sexual display is the joke
jokes.explanation: Good running extension of the McPoyle cringe. Mac needing to remind the brother of the familial relationship is funny precisely because the brother does not care.

jokes.text: Mac reluctantly agrees to call Margaret: 'Jesus, man, I'm sorry. Fine, I'll call her.'
jokes.setup: The McPoyle brother insists Mac call his sister Margaret after their bathroom encounter
jokes.punchline: Mac, under McPoyle pressure, agrees to 'call' Margaret — the social obligation of post-sex follow-up applied to the most grotesque possible scenario
jokes.explanation: Good beat — the social convention of 'calling after sex' applied to Margaret McPoyle is the joke. Mac's resignation is well-played.

jokes.text: Dee confronts the peacock girl: 'Hey, you, everybody thinks you're so hot, huh? You big hot bird. Well, I tell you what. You take it off and switch with me.'
jokes.setup: Dee, humiliated and covered in milk, decides to steal the peacock costume
jokes.punchline: Dee's confrontation escalates from jealousy ('everybody thinks you're so hot') to casual threat ('I'm not gonna beat the shit out of you, so let's go') while negotiating a costume switch
jokes.explanation: Good Dee moment — her negotiation technique (threat + rationalization) is in character. 'The second great thing for you is I'm not gonna beat the shit out of you' as a selling point is a nice touch.

jokes.text: Dee in the new costume: 'Call me a bird all night. Making fun, saying names. Well, let's see who's sexy now, dickwads. 'Cause I look good.'
jokes.setup: Dee has stolen the peacock girl's costume and now feels vindicated
jokes.punchline: Dee's victory speech — 'Let's see who's sexy now, dickwads. 'Cause I look good.' — delivered to no one in particular, is both pathetic and triumphant
jokes.explanation: The gap between Dee's triumphant declaration and the audience knowing she's still in a bird costume (a peacock) is the structural irony. 'Dickwads' as her victory-speech address is a great Dee touch.

jokes.text: McPoyle narrates: 'Knowing that Charlie was the weakest and by far the most vulnerable, she assumed he would be the easiest to take advantage of.'
jokes.setup: Dee is on a 'warpath to prove she's sexy' and decides to seduce one of the gang
jokes.punchline: The McPoyle's nature-documentary narration identifies Charlie as 'the weakest and most vulnerable' — a totally accurate but brutally honest assessment delivered with zero malice
jokes.explanation: The McPoyle's dispassionate narration framing Charlie as prey is excellent. The Nature Channel tone applied to the bar gang is a consistent joke throughout this section. 'Weakest and most vulnerable' as a clinical fact is both funny and sad for Charlie.

jokes.text: The reveal: 'That wasn't me. I switched costumes with Dennis. That was Dennis.'
jokes.setup: The McPoyle has just narrated that Dee took Charlie into the back office
jokes.punchline: Charlie reveals the costume switch means Dee actually had sex with Dennis, not Charlie — the entire episode's mystery pivots on this single costume-swap reveal
jokes.explanation: The structural payoff of the entire episode. The costume switch planted earlier pays off in a Rashomon-style reveal where both Dee and Dennis are victims of the same misidentification. The structure is excellent — everything in the episode (the costume argument, the switch, the peacock girl, Dee stealing the peacock costume) was setup for this. It's not a one-liner but a structural joke of the highest order.

jokes.text: 'You should see the look on your face. It's good enough to eat.'
jokes.setup: Dee has successfully lured 'Charlie' (actually Dennis) into the back office
jokes.punchline: Dee's predatory seduction line is 'it's good enough to eat' — an unsettling predatory framing of her prey's expression
jokes.explanation: The rewatch value is high — on rewatch Dennis's expression being 'good enough to eat' takes on a different meaning. Reasonably good seduction-reversal (Dee as predator) but not exceptional as a standalone line.

jokes.text: Beat: 'So Dee thinks that I'm the dad, but, Dennis, you're the dad!' — followed by McPoyle's 'Delightful.'
jokes.setup: Charlie has just realized Dennis is Dee's baby's father
jokes.punchline: McPoyle's response to the horror of sibling incest is a single, cheerful 'Delightful.' — the most inappropriate possible response
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best single-word jokes. 'Delightful.' as the McPoyle's response to implied incest is perfect — his affect is completely wrong for the situation, his word choice is Victorian-whimsical, and the economy is flawless. This is one word doing enormous work. High quotability.

jokes.text: Dennis's reaction: 'Oh, shit. I'm gonna be sick.' / Charlie: 'Go. Do it. Feel it. Let it out.'
jokes.setup: Dennis has just been told he is Dee's baby's father
jokes.punchline: Dennis physically vomits at the concept; Charlie's coaching ('Go. Do it. Feel it. Let it out.') turns Dennis's existential horror into a guided wellness exercise
jokes.explanation: Dennis physically vomiting at the idea of having slept with his sister is good dark comedy. Charlie's motivational coaching of the vomiting ('Feel it. Let it out.') adds the absurdist layer that elevates it.

jokes.text: 'Don't flush.' — McPoyle's instruction as Dennis vomits
jokes.setup: Dennis is vomiting in reaction to learning he may have fathered his sister's baby
jokes.punchline: 'Don't flush.' — the McPoyle's only contribution to this moment is a request not to flush, implying he wants to keep the vomit for some reason, delivered with total calm
jokes.explanation: Two words. Perfect. 'Don't flush.' in this context is the McPoyle at peak McPoyle — his grotesque, placid weirdness expressed in a single request. It tells you everything about him: he's unfazed by the incest reveal, he's interested in the vomit, and he communicates in the fewest possible syllables. Maximum economy (10/10 — it cannot be shorter). One of the episode's best jokes.

jokes.text: 'We got to get you and that monster that's in your gut down to Mexico A.S.A.P!'
jokes.setup: The gang has established Dennis is Dee's baby's father
jokes.punchline: Charlie's immediate plan is to take Dee to Mexico — his go-to solution to any problem — describing her baby as 'the monster that's in your gut'
jokes.explanation: Classic Charlie problem-solving — 'Mexico' as a universal solution. 'The monster that's in your gut' as a description of a fetus is a great dark-comedy line that also callbacks the bird/animal insults applied to Dee's baby.

jokes.text: Dee's revelation: she made the whole paternity story up to mess with them — 'I just told you that 'cause you were making fun of me for eating the sandwich.'
jokes.setup: The entire episode has been a paternity investigation treating Dee's pregnancy as a crisis
jokes.punchline: Dee casually reveals none of them are the father — she invented the story because they mocked her for eating a sandwich, and it worked perfectly
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best structural jokes. The entire episode's premise was invented by Dee to get back at the gang for sandwich-mocking. The disproportionate response (causing the entire gang to panic for a whole night over a sandwich insult) is perfectly in character for her. The callback to the opening sandwich scene closes the loop beautifully. High structure score.

jokes.text: 'You went into the back office with him, not me. You thought it was me 'cause you wanted sex from me! But you got sex from Dennis!'
jokes.setup: Dee denies having sex with Dennis
jokes.punchline: Charlie's explanation reveals the double humiliation: Dee wanted Charlie specifically, went after Charlie, and got Dennis — the insult being that she couldn't even correctly identify her target
jokes.explanation: Charlie's explanation of the situation is plot-driven rather than primarily comedic. The humor is in the specific embarrassment for Dee — she targeted Charlie (humiliating) and missed and got Dennis instead (doubly humiliating). Functional.

jokes.text: 'Have you guys been obsessing about this all night long?' / 'Yes!' / 'Yeah?' / 'Of course. We were running around trying to figure out who the father is.'
jokes.setup: Dee reveals her pregnancy announcement was a manipulation
jokes.punchline: The gang confirms with absolute enthusiasm that yes, they have been obsessing about this all night — their self-awareness about being played making it funnier
jokes.explanation: The mutual acknowledgment that they've been manipulated all night and confirm it willingly is good meta-comedy. Dee's manipulation working perfectly is a good character win for her. Functional payoff scene.

jokes.text: Dennis: 'Are you absolutely sure that you and I did not have sex and that that's not my —' / Dee: 'Uh, yeah.'
jokes.setup: Dee has just revealed the paternity story was a lie
jokes.punchline: Dennis, despite the relief, needs to double-check that he definitely did not have sex with his sister — his uncertainty is the horrifying punchline
jokes.explanation: The fact that Dennis cannot definitively rule out having had sex with his sister — he has to ASK — is one of the darkest and funniest beats in the episode. His browning-out is so complete that incest is a live possibility. The halting, unfinished sentence ('and that that's not my —') is excellent structure.

jokes.text: The gang's instant, euphoric relief — 'Whoa! Ho, ho! / Whoo!' — immediately followed by them all agreeing they don't care who the real father is
jokes.setup: The gang spent the entire episode in a panic about Dee's pregnancy
jokes.punchline: The moment they're off the hook, they're completely, instantly over it — 'Who cares? Who cares, right? It's no big deal.' The transition from terror to total indifference is instantaneous
jokes.explanation: Perfect character payoff. The gang's self-interest is so pure that relief and indifference are the same thing. 'Who cares, right?' from people who spent an entire night obsessing is the thesis of the whole show compressed into two seconds.

jokes.text: Dee tells them she won't reveal who the actual father is; the gang immediately claims they don't care — but Dee correctly notes 'You just said so. You were up all night.'
jokes.setup: Dee announces she won't reveal the real father's identity
jokes.punchline: The gang immediately says they don't care — 'Who gives a shit?' — but Dee calls their bluff: 'You all give a shit. You just said so.' Their rapid-cycling between caring and not caring is exposed
jokes.explanation: Good Dee moment — she gets a rare win by calling out the gang's transparent self-delusion. The rhythm of 'who cares / yeah but you just said / well now we don't' is well-structured.

jokes.text: Frank's physical reaction to the relief: 'I got to take a — Oh, Jesus. Whoo, ooh! Whoa, baby!'
jokes.setup: Frank has been under immense stress thinking he might be a grandfather
jokes.punchline: Frank's physical relief is so extreme it manifests as some kind of spontaneous bodily event — the specifics are left unclear and are funnier for it
jokes.explanation: Decent physical gag — Frank's body registering relief as a physical event is characteristically gross. The ambiguity about what exactly is happening is probably funnier than a specific answer. Moderate.

jokes.text: 'That is a load off my shoulders, man. I really dodged a bullet on that one. Well, we all did.' — the gang's underwhelming collective summary of the entire episode
jokes.setup: The gang has just discovered Dee's whole story was a manipulation
jokes.punchline: Their reaction to nearly being implicated in incestuous parenthood is 'That is a load off my shoulders' — the most blandly understated response possible
jokes.explanation: The deliberate banality of their response ('load off my shoulders') after a night of extreme emotional investment is in character. Functions as denouement humor.

jokes.text: The gang immediately pivots back to the museum plan: 'Hey, what about the museum?' / 'Yes!' / 'We could do it!' — the original plan from the opening scene
jokes.setup: The episode began with the gang excited to spend the night in a museum
jokes.punchline: With Dee's crisis resolved, the gang immediately reverts to its childlike museum excitement — the entire episode was a detour from their original plan
jokes.explanation: Perfect structural callback. The episode frame (museum night) is restored immediately after the crisis ends — the gang's childlike priorities are undimmed by what just happened. Good structural bookending.

jokes.text: The gang's escalating bird insults at Dee as they leave: 'You look like a turkey!' / 'You look like an ostrich!' / 'You are a big, fat, flightless bird!'
jokes.setup: The gang is heading to the museum, leaving Dee behind
jokes.punchline: Their farewell to Dee is a rapid-fire escalation of bird species: turkey → ostrich → 'big fat flightless bird' — each worse and more specific than the last
jokes.explanation: Good payoff to the bird running gag. The escalation from specific birds (turkey, ostrich) to the generic 'big fat flightless bird' — which somehow lands as the final button — is a fun ending. The aside about saving 'emu' for later is an extra meta-joke.

tmdb_overview: The gang gets a real scare after Dee reveals she's pregnant, forcing the guys to recall their last hazy Halloween party to determine who the father is.
